sections.title: Judgment on the Oppressors
observations: Micah begins this chapter by condemning those who devise iniquity and work evil on their beds. This highlights the premeditated nature of their sins, indicating that their actions are not mere mistakes but deliberate choices against God's will.

The imagery of coveting fields and seizing them through violence illustrates the social injustices prevalent in Israel. The wealthy and powerful are exploiting the vulnerable, which is a recurring theme in the prophetic literature.

sections.title: The Lord's Response
observations: God's response to the oppression is severe. He declares that He will devise disaster against these oppressors, emphasizing that divine justice will ultimately prevail.
The mention of the 'house of Jacob' signifies that God's judgment is not only on the oppressors but also on the entire nation for allowing such injustices to occur.

sections.title: Hope for the Remnant
observations: Despite the judgment, Micah offers a glimmer of hope. He speaks of a remnant that will be saved, indicating that God will preserve a faithful group amidst the judgment.
This remnant will be restored and will rise to lead the people back to righteousness, showcasing God's mercy even in the face of sin.

importantVerses.commentary: Woe to those who plan iniquity! This verse sets the tone for the chapter, highlighting the seriousness of premeditated sin and social injustice.
Arise and depart, for this is not your rest. This verse serves as a call to action for the oppressed, reminding them that their current state is not their final destination.

questions: What does Micah's condemnation of the oppressors reveal about God's character and His concern for justice?
How can we apply the message of hope for the remnant in our own lives today?
In what ways do we see similar injustices in our society, and how should we respond as believers?
